L17@P0: 1. Introduction
L18@P0: Nearly twenty years ago Mazur settled the question of which groups can occur as the group of
L19@P0: rational torsion points on an elliptic curve over Q, but the analogous question for Jacobian varieties
L20@P0: of curves over Q of genus greater than 1 remains open. Most of the work that has been done on this
L21@P0: question has centered on the problem of finding groups that do occur as rational torsion subgroups
L22@P0: of Jacobians. Several researchers have produced families of genus-2 curves whose Jacobians contain
L23@P0: various given groups in their rational torsion (see [21], [22], [25], [26], [33], and the summary in [29])
L24@P0: while others have constructed families of curves in which the size of the rational torsion subgroup
L25@P0: of the Jacobian increases as the genus of the curve increases (see [8], [9], [23], [24], [27], [28]). The
L26@P0: largest group of rational torsion heretofore known to exist on the Jacobian of a curve of genus 2
L27@P0: was a group of order 30; for genus-3 curves, the largest group had order 64.
L28@P0: In this paper we present many explicit families of curves of genus 2 and 3 whose Jacobians possess
L29@P0: large rational torsion subgroups. The strategy behind our constructions is to take a product of
L30@P0: elliptic curves, each with large rational torsion, and to find a curve whose Jacobian is isogenous to
L31@P0: the given product. Thus it is no surprise that the groups we list occur as torsion groups of abelian
L32@P0: varieties; rather, the point of interest is that they occur as torsion groups of Jacobian varieties.

L1@P0: Cover attacks for elliptic curves with prime order
L2@P0: Song Tian⋆

L6@P0: Abstract. We give a new approach to the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem over cubic extension fields Fq3 . It is based on a transfer:
L7@P0: First an Fq-rational (ℓ, ℓ, ℓ)-isogeny from the Weil restriction of the elliptic curve under consideration with respect to Fq3 /Fq to the Jacobian
L8@P0: variety of a genus three curve over Fq is applied and then the problem
L9@P0: is solved in the Jacobian via the index-calculus attacks. Although using
L10@P0: no covering maps in the construction of the desired homomorphism, this
L11@P0: method is, in a sense, a kind of cover attack. As a result, it is possible
L12@P0: to solve the discrete logarithm problem in some elliptic curve groups of
L13@P0: prime order over Fq3 in a time of O˜(q).
L14@P0: Keywords: cover attacks, discrete logarithm problem, Weil restriction,
L15@P0: isogeny, Jacobian variety
L16@P0: 1 Introduction
L17@P0: It is well known that the discrete logarithm problem in the groups of rational
L18@P0: points of elliptic curves over finite fields can be solved in a time which is given
L19@P0: by the square root of the group order. The corresponding algorithms in fact
L20@P0: work in all finite groups and are therefore called generic algorithms. Up to now
L21@P0: the fastest algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem in most of elliptic
L22@P0: curves are indeed the generic algorithms. Additionally, it is easy to construct
L23@P0: curves which are suited for cryptographic applications. For this reason, elliptic
L24@P0: curve cryptography is now widely used in practice, in particular for high-security
L25@P0: applications.
L26@P0: On the other hand, there are now some classes of elliptic curves known for
L27@P0: which the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem can be solved faster than
L28@P0: generic algorithms. In particular, it is well known that some elliptic curves over finite non-prime fields can be attacked with what is called cover attack by C. Diem
L29@P0: (see for example [4]).
L30@P0: Let E be an elliptic curve over an extension field Fqn . The idea of cover attacks is to reduce the discrete logarithm problem to the corresponding problem
L31@P0: in the Jacobian of a curve C of genus g ≥ n over Fq, where it can be solved in
L32@P0: a time of O˜(q
L33@P0: 2−2/g) via the index calculus method [9]. In order that the attack
L34@P0: ⋆ Song Tian is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under
L35@P0-1: Grant No. 61802401.is faster than generic attacks, one wants that the genus of C is small. For example, in the case that E(Fqn ) is prime (which is often the case in cryptographic
L36@P1: applications), it is optimal if g is equal to the extension degree n.
L37@P1: The first application of this idea is the GHS attack [3,8,10]. This attack is
L38@P1: only of relevance for relatively few curves. For example, if q is odd and n is prime
L39@P1: and not 3, 5 or 7, the genus of the resulting curve is always so large that one
L40@P1: can say that the attack fails. For n = 3, if we require C to be of genus 3, then
L41@P1: a necessary condition is that the elliptic curve has three rational points of order
L42@P1: 2 [3,13]. This therefore raises the natural question whether elliptic curves over
L43@P1: Fq
L44@P1: 3 with cofactor 1 or 2 can be attacked with cover attacks. A recent discussion
L45@P1: in [19] shows that C needs to be non-hyperelliptic if the elliptic curve has prime
L46@P1: order, and that when the cofactor is 2, it might be possible to construct a genus
L47@P1: 3 hyperelliptic curve C together with a degree 3 morphism C → E.
L48@P1: In this work, we give a new approach to the problem. The main idea is to
L49@P1: attempt to compute (ℓ, ℓ, ℓ)-isogenies from the Weil restriction of an elliptic curve
L50@P1: to the Jacobian of a genus 3 curve. This is motivated by the fact that principally
L51@P1: polarized abelian varieties of dimension 3 are the generalized Jacobian varieties
L52@P1: [15]. If we take such an isogeny for an elliptic curve E of prime order, we can
L53@P1: transfer the discrete logarithm problem from E(Fq
L54@P1: 3 ) to the Jacobian of a nonhyperelliptic curve over Fq, and solve it there in a time of O˜(q) [5]. In contrast,
L55@P1: if we apply the index-calculus method based on the summation polynomials to
L56@P1: the discrete logarithm problem in E(Fq
L57@P1: 3 ), then the complexity is O˜(q
L58@P1: 4/3
L59@P1: ) [7].
L60@P1: We note that the GHS attack [3,8] and the work [19] transfer the discrete
L61@P1: logarithm problem in a way which relies on the covering map: The homomorphism from the group under consideration to another group is the composition
L62@P1: of the pullback homomorphism induced by the covering map and the trace map
L63@P1: (or at the level of function fields of curves the composition of the conorm and
L64@P1: norm maps). This contrasts with the direct construction of a homomorphism in
L65@P1: the present work.
L66@P1: The method of computing the (ℓ, ℓ, ℓ)-isogenies is basically the same as the
L67@P1: one in [18]. The only difference is that the isogenies start from the Weil restriction of an elliptic curve instead of the Jacobian of a hyperelliptic curve.
L68@P1: We remark here that the most important notion for the computation is normal
L69@P1: Weil set, which is introduced by Shepherd-Barron in [17]. First, we use Weil sets
L70@P1: on the Weil restriction to construct a normal Weil set on the quotient of the
L71@P1: Weil restriction by a rational subgroup with certain property, from which we
L72@P1: can compute an equation for the resulting curve. The question then is, how to
L73@P1: compute the image in the Jacobian of this curve of a given point on the Weil
L74@P1: restriction? For this, we build a link between the normal Weil set on the quotient
L75@P1: and a normal Weil set on the Jacobian. Doing so allows us to know the values
L76@P1: of functions in the latter normal Weil set at the image point. Then we recover
L77@P1: the image point from these values by solving a system of polynomial equations.
L78@P1: The paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we give an introduction to

L83@P2: we recall normal Weil set and explain how to construct Weil sets on the Weil

L7: # Efficient scalar multiplication by isogeny decompositions
L8:

L18: ## Abstract
L19: On an elliptic curve, the degree of an isogeny corresponds essentially to the degrees of the polynomial expressions involved in its application. The multiplication-by-ℓ map [ℓ] has degree, therefore the complexity to directly evaluate [ℓ](P) is O(ℓ^{2}). For a small prime ℓ (= 2, 3) such that the additive binary representation provides no better performance, this represents the true cost of application of scalar multiplication.
L20: If an elliptic curve admits an isogeny φ of degree ℓ then the costs of computing φ(P) should in contrast be O(ℓ) field operations. Since we then have a product expression [ℓ] = φ̂φ, the existence of an ℓ-isogeny φ on an elliptic curve yields a theoretical improvement from O(ℓ^{2}) to O(ℓ) field operations for the evaluation of [ℓ](P) by naïve application of the defining polynomials. In this work we investigate actual improvements for small ℓ of this asymptotic complexity.
L21: For this purpose, we describe the general construction of families of curves with a suitable decomposition [ℓ] = φ̂φ, and provide explicit examples of such a family of curves with simple decomposition for [3].
L22: Finally we derive a new tripling algorithm to find complexity improvements to triplication on a curve in certain projective coordinate systems, then combine this new operation to non-adjacent forms for ℓ-adic expansions in order to obtain an improved strategy for scalar multiplication on elliptic curves.

L78: title = "Efficient scalar multiplication by isogeny decompositions",
L79: abstract = "On an elliptic curve, the degree of an isogeny corresponds essentially to the degrees of the polynomial expressions involved in its application. The multiplication-by-ℓ map [ℓ] has degree, therefore the complexity to directly evaluate [ℓ](P) is O(ℓ2). For a small prime ℓ (= 2, 3) such that the additive binary representation provides no better performance, this represents the true cost of application of scalar multiplication.
L80: If an elliptic curve admits an isogeny φ of degree ℓ then the costs of computing φ(P) should in contrast be O(ℓ) field operations. Since we then have a product expression [ℓ] = {\^φ}φ, the existence of an ℓ-isogeny φ on an elliptic curve yields a theoretical improvement from O(ℓ2) to O(ℓ) field operations for the evaluation of [ℓ](P) by na{\"i}ve application of the defining polynomials. In this work we investigate actual improvements for small ℓ of this asymptotic complexity.
L81: For this purpose, we describe the general construction of families of curves with a suitable decomposition [ℓ] = {\^φ}φ, and provide explicit examples of such a family of curves with simple decomposition for [3].
L82: Finally we derive a new tripling algorithm to find complexity improvements to triplication on a curve in certain projective coordinate systems, then combine this new operation to non-adjacent forms for ℓ-adic expansions in order to obtain an improved strategy for scalar multiplication on elliptic curves.",
